questions.q: How does this lesson define maintainability?
options: How visually polished a solution looks to an end user
How easily and safely a solution can be understood, modified, and extended by someone other than its original builder, including that same builder much later
How quickly the original developer can build the first version
The number of custom objects a solution uses
questions.explain: Maintainability is about the cost and safety of future changes, not how the solution looks or performs on day one -- a solution can be functional and still poorly maintainable.

questions.q: What is 'Flow sprawl,' as described in this lesson, and why is it a maintainability risk?
options: A single well-documented Flow that handles all automation for an object, which is actually good practice

Dozens of record-triggered Flows on the same object built by different people with no naming convention or shared understanding, which can be harder to maintain than tangled Apex because there's no single file to read
A Flow that calls too many subflows, which is always forbidden
An error that occurs only in Experience Cloud sites
questions.explain: Flow sprawl is the accumulation of many loosely related, undocumented Flows on one object -- the lesson argues this can be even harder to maintain than undisciplined code, since there's no single place to read the full picture.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why are Custom Labels, Custom Settings, and Custom Metadata Types described as maintainability tools?
options: They keep changeable configuration values out of hardcoded automation logic, so a business-rule change doesn't require touching and re-testing the logic itself
They are required by Salesforce for every Flow to function at all
They replace the need for naming conventions entirely
They only matter for data-volume scalability, not maintainability
questions.explain: Externalizing changeable values into these configuration mechanisms means a business-rule change is a configuration update, not a logic change that requires re-testing and re-deploying automation.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a hardcoded value buried inside a Flow's decision element is a maintainability trap?
options: Because hardcoded values always cause immediate runtime errors
Because the next person to touch the Flow has no way to discover that value exists without opening and reading every element
Because Flows are not allowed to contain decision elements
Because hardcoded values are automatically flagged by Salesforce's UI
questions.explain: A hardcoded value buried deep in automation is invisible to the next maintainer unless they manually inspect every element -- exactly the kind of hidden cost that erodes maintainability.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that treating maintainability as a 'cleanup sprint to do later' tends not to work?
options: Because cleanup sprints are illegal under Salesforce's governance model

Because cleanup sprints compete for the same time as new feature requests and rarely win, so maintainability decisions are more durable when made continuously, in the moment, on every individual build decision
Because maintainability can only be improved by a full platform migration
Because Salesforce automatically cleans up Flow sprawl on a schedule
questions.explain: The lesson argues that deferred cleanup rarely happens in practice because it competes with new feature work, so the more durable approach treats maintainability as a small decision made at the time each piece of automation or naming choice is created.
